old:
Cost factors: relative unit labour costs, the exchange rate (a weaker currency cheapens exports), relative inflation, and productivity, which lowers cost per unit.

Non-cost factors: innovation and technology, quality and branding that command premium prices, and infrastructure and logistics — transport, energy and digital networks that keep firms efficient.

Cost factors

old:
Economic growth in developing countries raises incomes and employment, pulling people over the fixed threshold. Government policies — welfare benefits, subsidies and public services — support the poorest directly.

Global factors — trade, foreign aid and investment — shape poverty in developing countries, while natural disasters and conflicts push it the other way by destroying livelihoods and infrastructure.
new:
• Economic growth in developing countries raises incomes and employment, pulling people over the fixed threshold.
  • Government policies — welfare benefits, subsidies and public services — support the poorest directly.
  • Global factors — trade, foreign aid and investment — shape poverty in developing countries.
  • Natural disasters and conflicts push it the other way by destroying livelihoods and infrastructure.

old:
Because relative poverty is measured against median income, it moves with the income distribution: the skills gap in education drives wage disparities; demographic changes — ageing populations, shifting household composition — alter who falls below the line.

Government tax and welfare policy redistributes income directly, and labour market changes — unemployment, underemployment and low wages — push relative poverty up.
new:
Because relative poverty is measured against median income, it moves with the income distribution:

  • The skills gap in education drives wage disparities.
  • Demographic changes — ageing populations, shifting household composition — alter who falls below the line.
  • Government tax and welfare policy redistributes income directly.
  • Labour market changes — unemployment, underemployment and low wages — push relative poverty up.

old:
Education and skills — unequal access drives wage disparities. The tax system — progressive taxation redistributes towards lower incomes. Welfare payments — support the disposable income of the poorest. The minimum wage — lifts the lowest earners. Trade unions — negotiate better pay for low- and middle-income workers.

And the distribution of assets itself: who already holds property and financial investments shapes the income they generate.
new:
• Education and skills — unequal access drives wage disparities.
  • The tax system — progressive taxation redistributes towards lower incomes.
  • Welfare payments — support the disposable income of the poorest.
  • The minimum wage — lifts the lowest earners.
  • Trade unions — negotiate better pay for low- and middle-income workers.
  • The distribution of assets itself: who already holds property and financial investments shapes the income they generate.

old:
The UN's Human Development Index combines three equally weighted elements: health (life expectancy at birth), education (mean years of schooling for adults, expected years for children) and income (real GNI per capita at PPP, adjusting for cost-of-living differences).

Countries score between 0 and 1 — Norway 0.961, Niger 0.394 — with higher scores meaning higher human development.
new:
The UN's Human Development Index combines three equally weighted elements:

  • Health (life expectancy at birth).
  • Education (mean years of schooling for adults, expected years for children).
  • Income (real GNI per capita at PPP, adjusting for cost-of-living differences).

Countries score between 0 and 1 — Norway 0.961, Niger 0.394 — with higher scores meaning higher human development.

old:
The Multidimensional Poverty Index (MPI) across health, education and living standards; the Inequality-adjusted HDI (IHDI), discounting the HDI for inequality; GNI per capita; and access to clean water and sanitation.

Plus environmental indicators (emissions, deforestation, biodiversity loss — is development sustainable?), the Human Poverty Index and the Social Progress Index.
new:
• The Multidimensional Poverty Index (MPI) across health, education and living standards.
  • The Inequality-adjusted HDI (IHDI), discounting the HDI for inequality.
  • GNI per capita.
  • Access to clean water and sanitation.
  • Environmental indicators (emissions, deforestation, biodiversity loss — is development sustainable?).
  • The Human Poverty Index and the Social Progress Index.

old:
Demographics — rapid population growth strains resources, ageing shrinks the workforce. Debt — servicing it diverts resources from investment and scares off FDI. Access to credit and banking — without it, individuals and firms cannot fund productive investment. Infrastructure — poor transport, communication and energy raise costs and cut off markets.

Education and skills build the human capital growth needs — and an absence of property rights undermines it all: without secure legal ownership, why invest or innovate?
new:
• Demographics — rapid population growth strains resources, ageing shrinks the workforce.
  • Debt — servicing it diverts resources from investment and scares off FDI.
  • Access to credit and banking — without it, individuals and firms cannot fund productive investment.
  • Infrastructure — poor transport, communication and energy raise costs and cut off markets.
  • Education and skills build the human capital growth needs.
  • An absence of property rights undermines it all: without secure legal ownership, why invest or innovate?

old:
Corruption — diverts resources from productive investment, distorts decisions and raises costs. Poor governance and political instability — create uncertainty, deter foreign investment and waste resources.

Conflict and war — destroy physical capital and can set development back decades. And geography — being landlocked or facing difficult terrain raises transport costs and weakens trade competitiveness.
new:
• Corruption — diverts resources from productive investment, distorts decisions and raises costs.
  • Poor governance and political instability — create uncertainty, deter foreign investment and waste resources.
  • Conflict and war — destroy physical capital and can set development back decades.
  • Geography — being landlocked or facing difficult terrain raises transport costs and weakens trade competitiveness.

old:
Development of human capital (education and healthcare), protectionism (shelter domestic industries while they grow), managed exchange rates (stability for exporters and investors), infrastructure development (transport, energy, communications), joint ventures with global companies (investment and technology transfer), and buffer stock schemes (stabilise commodity prices).

All are government-led actions designed to correct market failure and direct development.
new:
• Development of human capital (education and healthcare).
  • Protectionism (shelter domestic industries while they grow).
  • Managed exchange rates (stability for exporters and investors).
  • Infrastructure development (transport, energy, communications).
  • Joint ventures with global companies (investment and technology transfer).
  • Buffer stock schemes (stabilise commodity prices).

All are government-led actions designed to correct market failure and direct development.

old:
The Lewis model: explains how labour from the agricultural sector can be transferred to the industrial sector, leading to economic growth and development — industry adds more value, raising real national income and living standards.

Its limits: it assumes surplus agricultural labour, which may not exist, and ignores industrialisation's negative externalities — environmental degradation and social inequality. Related routes: tourism (foreign exchange, but fragile) and primary industries (comparative advantage, but volatile).
new:
The Lewis model: explains how labour from the agricultural sector can be transferred to the industrial sector, leading to economic growth and development — industry adds more value, raising real national income and living standards.

Its limits:

  • It assumes surplus agricultural labour, which may not exist.
  • It ignores industrialisation's negative externalities — environmental degradation and social inequality.

Related routes: tourism (foreign exchange, but fragile) and primary industries (comparative advantage, but volatile).

old:
Fairtrade guarantees minimum prices and premiums, raising producer incomes — but reaches few producers, and higher consumer prices limit demand. Aid (grants, soft loans, humanitarian support) funds vital projects — but can create dependency, be misallocated, or serve donors' political agendas.

Debt relief frees resources for development and improves creditworthiness — but leaves structural problems untouched, and without fiscal discipline new debt simply accumulates.
new:
• Fairtrade guarantees minimum prices and premiums, raising producer incomes — but reaches few producers, and higher consumer prices limit demand.
  • Aid (grants, soft loans, humanitarian support) funds vital projects — but can create dependency, be misallocated, or serve donors' political agendas.
  • Debt relief frees resources for development and improves creditworthiness — but leaves structural problems untouched, and without fiscal discipline new debt simply accumulates.

old:
The World Bank aims to reduce poverty through long-term loans for infrastructure and development projects, plus technical assistance. The IMF promotes global financial stability with short-term loans for balance-of-payments crises — usually with conditions, such as structural adjustment programmes and austerity.

NGOs — non-profits independent of governments, like Oxfam — deliver aid, run development projects and advocate on specific issues such as education, healthcare and human rights.
new:
• The World Bank aims to reduce poverty through long-term loans for infrastructure and development projects, plus technical assistance.
  • The IMF promotes global financial stability with short-term loans for balance-of-payments crises — usually with conditions, such as structural adjustment programmes and austerity.
  • NGOs — non-profits independent of governments, like Oxfam — deliver aid, run development projects and advocate on specific issues such as education, healthcare and human rights.

old:
Facilitate saving — deposits, bonds and equities let households and firms earn a return and accumulate wealth (and, per Harrod-Domar, savings fund growth). Lend to businesses and individuals for investment and consumption. Facilitate the exchange of goods and services through money and payment systems.

Provide forward markets in currencies and commodities, letting firms hedge price risk. And provide a market for equities, so firms can raise capital by issuing shares.
new:
• Facilitate saving — deposits, bonds and equities let households and firms earn a return and accumulate wealth (and, per Harrod-Domar, savings fund growth).
  • Lend to businesses and individuals for investment and consumption.
  • Facilitate the exchange of goods and services through money and payment systems.
  • Provide forward markets in currencies and commodities, letting firms hedge price risk.
  • Provide a market for equities, so firms can raise capital by issuing shares.

old:
Moral hazard: occurs when individuals or institutions take on excessive risk because they do not bear the full consequences of their actions — banks expecting bailouts, or the insured taking chances they otherwise would not.

Speculation: buying assets purely expecting prices to rise, inflating bubbles that burst into instability. Market rigging: manipulating markets for private gain — the LIBOR scandal — distorting prices and destroying trust.
new:
Moral hazard: occurs when individuals or institutions take on excessive risk because they do not bear the full consequences of their actions — banks expecting bailouts, or the insured taking chances they otherwise would not.

Speculation: buying assets purely expecting prices to rise, inflating bubbles that burst into instability.

Market rigging: manipulating markets for private gain — the LIBOR scandal — distorting prices and destroying trust.

old:
Systemic risk — trouble in one institution spreads through the whole system into financial crisis. Loss of confidence — collapsing trust brings bank runs and panic.

Real economic damage — recession, unemployment and lost output follow financial failure. And inequity — taxpayers end up bearing the cost of bailing out private institutions.
new:
• Systemic risk — trouble in one institution spreads through the whole system into financial crisis.
  • Loss of confidence — collapsing trust brings bank runs and panic.
  • Real economic damage — recession, unemployment and lost output follow financial failure.
  • Inequity — taxpayers end up bearing the cost of bailing out private institutions.

old:
Implementing monetary policy — the Bank of England's MPC sets interest rates (and QE at the zero lower bound) to meet the government's 2% CPI inflation target. Banker to the government — managing its accounts and issuing its debt.

Banker to the banks — central banks act as a lender of last resort to commercial banks and other financial institutions in times of financial stress, providing emergency funding in a liquidity crisis. And regulating the banking system.
new:
• Implementing monetary policy — the Bank of England's MPC sets interest rates (and QE at the zero lower bound) to meet the government's 2% CPI inflation target.
  • Banker to the government — managing its accounts and issuing its debt.
  • Banker to the banks — central banks act as a lender of last resort to commercial banks and other financial institutions in times of financial stress, providing emergency funding in a liquidity crisis.
  • Regulating the banking system.

old:
Current expenditure: day-to-day spending on public sector wages, such as payments to teachers and nurses, and on the consumption of goods and services such as medicines and utilities.

Capital expenditure: long-term investment in infrastructure — roads, hospitals, schools — raising productive potential. Transfer payments: payments with no good or service received in return — pensions, benefits, subsidies — which redistribute income but do not directly add to GDP.
new:
Current expenditure: day-to-day spending on public sector wages, such as payments to teachers and nurses, and on the consumption of goods and services such as medicines and utilities.

Capital expenditure: long-term investment in infrastructure — roads, hospitals, schools — raising productive potential.

Transfer payments: payments with no good or service received in return — pensions, benefits, subsidies — which redistribute income but do not directly add to GDP.

old:
Economic growth lifts tax revenue and cuts transfer payments, freeing spending for services. Demographic change — an ageing population — raises pension and healthcare spending. Political priorities shift money between sectors.

External shocks — recessions, pandemics — force up transfers and stimulus. And technological change alters what public services cost and need, such as digital infrastructure.
new:
• Economic growth lifts tax revenue and cuts transfer payments, freeing spending for services.
  • Demographic change — an ageing population — raises pension and healthcare spending.
  • Political priorities shift money between sectors.
  • External shocks — recessions, pandemics — force up transfers and stimulus.
  • Technological change alters what public services cost and need, such as digital infrastructure.

old:
For a bigger state: infrastructure, education and health spending raise productivity and LRAS; services and transfers lift living standards and equality.

Against: crowding out — government borrowing bids up interest rates, squeezing private investment and consumption — and higher spending eventually means higher taxes, cutting disposable income. The verdict turns on what the money buys: capital spending that grows the economy, or current spending that must be financed forever.
new:
For a bigger state: infrastructure, education and health spending raise productivity and LRAS; services and transfers lift living standards and equality.

Against:

  • Crowding out — government borrowing bids up interest rates, squeezing private investment and consumption.
  • Higher spending eventually means higher taxes, cutting disposable income.

The verdict turns on what the money buys: capital spending that grows the economy, or current spending that must be financed forever.

old:
Progressive: a tax where the percentage of income paid in tax rises as income rises — income tax, inheritance tax. Proportional: the percentage stays constant at every income. Regressive: the percentage falls as income rises — VAT and duties on tobacco and alcohol.

Direct taxes (on income or profits: income tax, corporation tax, National Insurance) tend to be progressive; indirect taxes (on spending: VAT, excise duties) tend to be regressive.
new:
• Progressive: a tax where the percentage of income paid in tax rises as income rises — income tax, inheritance tax.
  • Proportional: the percentage stays constant at every income.
  • Regressive: the percentage falls as income rises — VAT and duties on tobacco and alcohol.

Direct taxes (on income or profits: income tax, corporation tax, National Insurance) tend to be progressive; indirect taxes (on spending: VAT, excise duties) tend to be regressive.

old:
A fiscal deficit: government spending exceeds taxation revenue in a given period — it resets each year. The national debt: the total amount of money that a government owes to creditors — the accumulation of past deficits and surpluses over time.

A cyclical deficit follows the economic cycle, widening in recession and narrowing in boom. A structural deficit persists even at potential output — a fundamental imbalance the cycle will not fix.
new:
A fiscal deficit: government spending exceeds taxation revenue in a given period — it resets each year.

The national debt: the total amount of money that a government owes to creditors — the accumulation of past deficits and surpluses over time.

A cyclical deficit follows the economic cycle, widening in recession and narrowing in boom.

A structural deficit persists even at potential output — a fundamental imbalance the cycle will not fix.

old:
Economic growth — strong growth lifts tax revenue and trims welfare spending. Interest rates — higher rates raise the cost of servicing existing debt. Government spending priorities and taxation policy set the balance directly.

Then the pressures: demographic change (ageing populations demand more welfare and healthcare) and external shocks — crises, pandemics, disasters — that force spending up as revenue falls.
new:
• Economic growth — strong growth lifts tax revenue and trims welfare spending.
  • Interest rates — higher rates raise the cost of servicing existing debt.
  • Government spending priorities and taxation policy set the balance directly.

Then the pressures:

  • Demographic change (ageing populations demand more welfare and healthcare).
  • External shocks — crises, pandemics, disasters — that force spending up as revenue falls.

old:
Economic stability — eroding confidence raises borrowing costs and deters investment; persistent deficits risk credit-rating downgrades and, at the limit, a debt crisis. Intergenerational equity — future taxpayers inherit the repayments.

Inflation — financing deficits by printing money debases the currency. And policy flexibility — a heavily indebted government has little fiscal room left when the next shock arrives.
new:
• Economic stability — eroding confidence raises borrowing costs and deters investment; persistent deficits risk credit-rating downgrades and, at the limit, a debt crisis.
  • Intergenerational equity — future taxpayers inherit the repayments.
  • Inflation — financing deficits by printing money debases the currency.
  • Policy flexibility — a heavily indebted government has little fiscal room left when the next shock arrives.

old:
Deficits and debt: fiscal austerity (spending cuts, tax rises) to restore confidence; structural reforms — labour markets, pensions, public-service efficiency — to grow revenue; and debt restructuring with creditors: longer repayment, lower rates, or partial write-off.

Poverty and inequality: progressive taxation, social welfare programmes, and investment in education and healthcare to raise social mobility.
new:
Deficits and debt

  • Fiscal austerity (spending cuts, tax rises) to restore confidence.
  • Structural reforms — labour markets, pensions, public-service efficiency — to grow revenue.
  • Debt restructuring with creditors: longer repayment, lower rates, or partial write-off.

Poverty and inequality: progressive taxation, social welfare programmes, and investment in education and healthcare to raise social mobility.

old:
Tools: regulation (antitrust, environmental and labour standards), taxation — including rules against transfer pricing, where an MNC prices sales between its own subsidiaries to shift profits into low-tax jurisdictions — and international cooperation through the OECD and UN.

The limits: global firms can relocate to friendlier regimes, exploit regulatory arbitrage between countries, and effective control ultimately requires international coordination no single government can impose.
new:
Tools:

  • Regulation (antitrust, environmental and labour standards).
  • Taxation — including rules against transfer pricing, where an MNC prices sales between its own subsidiaries to shift profits into low-tax jurisdictions.
  • International cooperation through the OECD and UN.

The limits:

  • Global firms can relocate to friendlier regimes.
  • They can exploit regulatory arbitrage between countries.
  • Effective control ultimately requires international coordination no single government can impose.

old:
Inaccurate information — policy is set on data and forecasts that are often wrong or incomplete, producing unintended consequences. Risks and uncertainties — economic shocks, geopolitical events and shifting global markets defy prediction.

And an inability to control external shocks — global crises arrive regardless of domestic policy; governments can only respond, with monetary, fiscal and exchange-rate tools whose effects come with lags. Policy in an interconnected world is damage limitation as much as control.
new:
• Inaccurate information — policy is set on data and forecasts that are often wrong or incomplete, producing unintended consequences.
  • Risks and uncertainties — economic shocks, geopolitical events and shifting global markets defy prediction.
  • An inability to control external shocks — global crises arrive regardless of domestic policy; governments can only respond, with monetary, fiscal and exchange-rate tools whose effects come with lags.

Policy in an interconnected world is damage limitation as much as control.
